frameworks.name: Google Business Profile Lead Gen Framework
frameworks.definition: A three-step local-services lead generation system: (1) verify and rank a Google Business Profile with reviews, (2) answer inbound calls with a scripted close, (3) outsource fulfillment to a subcontractor on a 60-40 revenue split.

frameworks.name: Inspection-Fee Close Sequence
frameworks.definition: A two-step close for local service calls: first close the inspection appointment with a nominal fee ($60) to create skin-in-the-game commitment; let the on-site subcontractor close the full job — eliminating the need for the call-taker to know anything about the service.

claims.text: Eric (local services operator, 2023-2024) argues that charging a small inspection fee ($60 in his plumbing example) before committing to a site visit confirms buyer commitment and raises the probability that the subcontractor closes the full job on-site to near 99%, because the prospect has already paid to engage and faces a sunk-cost disincentive to call a second provider.
claims.speaker: Eric
conditions: local services where on-site diagnosis is required before pricing
emergency or high-need service context
claims.mechanism: By paying an inspection fee, the prospect commits financially; backing out means paying $60 and starting over with a new vendor — a cost most prospects rationally avoid, so the on-site visit becomes the effective close.

claims.text: Eric (local services operator, 2023-2024) argues that local service businesses such as plumbing are easy to outcompete in sales because the owners are tradespeople, not salespeople — they answer calls unprofessionally, miss calls frequently, and do not follow up — making basic call professionalism a structural competitive advantage.
claims.speaker: Eric
conditions: local trade service businesses operated by working tradespeople
markets where call-answering is not professionalized
claims.mechanism: Tradespeople optimize for service delivery, not lead conversion; their communication habits (informal greetings, missed calls, no follow-up) lower customer trust and close rates, leaving room for a dedicated call operator to capture a disproportionate share of inbound demand.
bounded_by: Does not apply to franchise or chain service businesses with professional call centers
Advantage erodes as more lead-gen operators enter the same market

examples.text: Eric played a recorded inbound plumbing call lasting 1 minute and 56 seconds. The caller reported his hot water was not working. Eric opened with 'Hey, this is Eric from [company name] speaking, how can I help you?' The caller explained the issue. Eric responded that a technician would need to come out for a $60 inspection fee (waived if the customer proceeds with the repair). The caller's only objection was timing — the afternoon slot did not work. Eric offered 1 p.m. the next day. The caller agreed, gave his address, and the call ended. Eric collected ~$300 from the resulting job.

Eric described a single large-scope plumbing emergency where the plumber charged approximately $5,000 for the job. At the 40% margin split, Eric earned approximately $2,000 from a single two-minute call. He cited this as an example of the upside tail of the model, contrasting it with the more typical $300 profit per average $700 job.

Eric showed a Google Business Profile for plumbing in his city that was ranking #1 in organic results. The profile had 190 reviews (acknowledged by Eric as fake). In the prior week, the profile received 21 inbound calls despite Eric being less active. He used this as evidence that a single well-optimized profile generates sufficient volume to hit $1,000/day on its own.

practices.text: Answer inbound calls with your name and company name: 'Hey, this is [Name] from [Company Name] speaking, how can I help you?' — this sets a professional tone that most local trade competitors lack.
If you miss an inbound call, at minimum send a text message back immediately; preferably call back. Missed calls that receive no follow-up are effectively lost to a competitor.
Charge a nominal inspection fee ($60 in Eric's plumbing example) that is waived if the customer proceeds with the repair; never give a price estimate over the phone for services requiring diagnosis.
When sourcing subcontractors, call approximately 10 local providers per trade and ask each if they will accept contracted work on a 60-40 split; expect roughly 3 out of 10 to agree.

To rank a Google Business Profile, verify the listing and accumulate reviews (Eric describes using fake reviews); add good photos; repeat the profile setup across multiple geographic markets or service types to multiply lead volume.
Schedule subcontractor visits for the same day whenever possible; same-day service matches customer urgency and enables same-day payment collection.
